subject: maths
title: Angle chasing
summary: Finding unknown angles through multi-step chains that combine parallel lines, triangles, isosceles triangles, exterior angles, construction lines and algebra, with a reason for every step.
body:
**Angle chasing** means finding a hidden angle by moving through a diagram one step at a time, using one angle rule at each step, like following clues. Builders use it to check roof trusses, and it is the heart of most geometry problems in selective and competition tests.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can find unknown angles in diagrams that need several steps, combining the straight-line, point, vertically opposite, parallel-line, triangle and isosceles rules, and give a reason for every step.

## Before you start

This lesson builds on Angles at a point and vertically opposite angles (Year 7), Angles and parallel lines (Year 7) and Triangles (Year 7). You should already know the F, Z and C rules and that the angles of a triangle add to 180°.

**Warm-up**

1. Two angles of a triangle are 47° and 68°. Find the third angle.
2. Two co-interior angles lie between parallel lines. One is 104°. Find the other.

*Answers:* 1. 180 − 47 − 68 = 65° 2. 180 − 104 = 76°

## Think of it like this

### A treasure hunt

In a treasure hunt, each clue sends you to the next one until you reach the prize. In angle chasing, the given angle is the first clue, each rule moves you to a new angle, and the angle you want is the treasure.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a treasure hunt has one fixed path, but in angle chasing there are often several different routes to the same angle, and you are allowed to draw your own extra lines to make a shortcut.

## Key ideas

### Your toolkit of rules

Every step in a chase uses one of these rules. Write the reason in brackets after each step.

| Rule | Reason to write |
|---|---|
| Angles on a straight line add to 180° | (angles on a straight line) |
| Angles at a point add to 360° | (angles at a point) |
| Vertically opposite angles are equal | (vertically opposite) |
| Corresponding (F) and alternate (Z) angles are equal | (corresponding, AB ∥ CD) / (alternate, AB ∥ CD) |
| Co-interior (C) angles add to 180° | (co-interior, AB ∥ CD) |
| Angles in a triangle add to 180° | (angle sum of triangle) |
| Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal | (isosceles triangle) |
| An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles | (exterior angle of triangle) |

### Isosceles triangles hide equal angles

Matching **tick marks** on two sides mean those sides are equal, so the triangle is **isosceles**. The two angles opposite the equal sides — the **base angles** — are equal. If you know the angle between the equal sides (the **apex angle**), each base angle is (180 − apex) ÷ 2.

![An isosceles triangle ABC with tick marks showing AB equals AC; the apex angle A is 40° and the base angles B and C are both 70°](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/angle-chasing-iso.svg)

### The exterior angle shortcut

If you extend one side of a triangle, the angle outside the triangle is an **exterior angle**. It equals the sum of the two **interior opposite angles** (the two angles of the triangle that are not next to it). Why? The exterior angle and the angle beside it make 180° (straight line), and the three angles of the triangle also make 180°. Take away the shared angle from both and what is left must match: exterior = a + b.

![Triangle ABC with side BC extended to D; the angles at A and B are labelled a and b and the exterior angle ACD is labelled a + b](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/angle-chasing-ext.svg)

### Write a chain, and mark the diagram

Name angles with three letters (∠ABC is the angle at B). Each line says what you found and why, e.g. "∠ACB = 68° (angles on a straight line)". Write each angle you find onto the diagram — the next step usually uses it.

### Construction lines

When no rule connects the angles, draw a **construction line** — an extra line you add yourself. For a bent line between two parallel lines, draw a dashed line through the bend, parallel to the other two. This makes two Z shapes, so the bend angle = p + q.

![Two parallel lines AB and CD with a bent line from A to E to C between them; a dashed line through E is parallel to both; angle BAE and the top part of angle AEC are both p, and angle DCE and the bottom part of angle AEC are both q](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/angle-chasing-bent.svg)

### Working backwards with algebra

When angles are written with letters, such as x° and (x + 20)°, use a rule to write an equation, solve it, and then substitute back to find the angle the question asks for. Always check that the angles make sense (no negative or zero angles).

## Worked examples

### Example 1

In triangle ABC, AB = AC and ∠BAC = 52°. Side BC is extended to D. Find ∠ACD.

![Isosceles triangle ABC with AB equal to AC marked by ticks, apex angle A of 52°, and side BC extended to D; the exterior angle ACD is marked with a question mark](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/angle-chasing-ex1.svg)

Step 1: AB = AC, so the base angles are equal: ∠ABC = ∠ACB = (180 − 52) ÷ 2 = 64° (isosceles triangle).
Step 2: ∠ACD = 180 − 64 = 116° (angles on a straight line).
Check with the exterior angle rule: 52 + 64 = 116 ✓

### Example 2

AB ∥ CD. Point E lies between the lines. ∠BAE = 41° and ∠DCE = 33°. Find ∠AEC.

![Parallel lines AB and CD with a bent line A to E to C; angle BAE is 41°, angle DCE is 33° and angle AEC is marked with a question mark](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/angle-chasing-ex2.svg)

Step 1: Draw a construction line through E parallel to AB (and so also parallel to CD) — to make two Z shapes.
Step 2: The top part of ∠AEC = 41° (alternate angles, AB ∥ the new line).
Step 3: The bottom part of ∠AEC = 33° (alternate angles, CD ∥ the new line).
Step 4: ∠AEC = 41 + 33 = 74°.

### Example 3

The top line and the bottom line are parallel. P is on the top line and Q and R are on the bottom line. The angle between the top line (to the left of P) and PQ is 58°, and ∠QPR = 49°. Find y = ∠PRQ.

![Two parallel lines; triangle PQR has P on the top line and Q and R on the bottom line; the angle between the top line on the left and PQ is 58°, angle QPR is 49°, and angle PRQ is y](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/angle-chasing-ex3.svg)

Step 1: ∠PQR = 58° (alternate angles, the lines are parallel) — the Z joins the 58° to the angle at Q.
Step 2: y = 180 − 58 − 49 = 73 (angle sum of triangle PQR).
Check: 58 + 49 + 73 = 180 ✓

### Example 4

In triangle ABC, ∠A = x° and ∠B = 2x°. Side BC is extended to D and the exterior angle ∠ACD = 132°. Find x and all three angles of the triangle.

![Triangle ABC with angle A labelled x°, angle B labelled 2x°, and side BC extended to D with exterior angle ACD of 132°](/diagrams/y7/maths-advanced/angle-chasing-ex4.svg)

Step 1: The exterior angle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles, so x + 2x = 132.
Step 2: 3x = 132, so x = 44 — divide both sides by 3.
Step 3: ∠A = 44°, ∠B = 88°, ∠ACB = 180 − 132 = 48° (angles on a straight line).
Check: 44 + 88 + 48 = 180 ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Using parallel-line rules without parallel lines.** It happens because many diagrams look parallel. Fix: only use F, Z or C if the lines have arrow marks or the question says they are parallel.
- **Picking the wrong pair of equal angles in an isosceles triangle.** The equal angles are opposite the equal sides, not next to the apex. Fix: put a finger on each ticked side and look at the angle across from it.
- **Stopping one step too early.** You find x or a base angle and forget what was asked. Fix: reread the question before answering.
- **Adding the exterior angle into the triangle.** The exterior angle is outside the triangle, so it is not part of the 180°. Fix: use the angle beside it (180 − exterior) for the triangle sum.

## Tips to remember

- **"Clue to clue":** write every angle you find on the diagram — each one is a new clue. (Made-up memory trick.)
- **Bent line = add:** when a line bends between two parallel lines and points away from them, the bend angle is the sum of the two angles at the parallel lines. Draw the dashed parallel line through the bend to see why.
- **Outside = the other two inside:** an exterior angle of a triangle equals the two interior angles that are not next to it.
- **Ticks talk:** tick marks on sides mean equal sides, and equal sides mean equal opposite angles.
- **Self-check:** add up the angles of every triangle and every straight line in your finished diagram. Each must make 180°.

## Key terms

- **Angle chasing** — finding an unknown angle through a chain of steps, each using one angle rule.
- **Isosceles triangle** — a triangle with two equal sides; the angles opposite them (base angles) are equal.
- **Apex angle** — the angle between the two equal sides of an isosceles triangle.
- **Exterior angle** — the angle between one side of a triangle and the extension of the next side.
- **Interior opposite angles** — the two angles inside a triangle that are not next to a given exterior angle.
- **Construction line** — an extra line you draw yourself to help solve a problem.

## Summary

- Angle chasing finds an angle step by step, with one rule and one reason per step.
- Base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal: each is (180 − apex) ÷ 2.
- An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
- A construction line parallel to two parallel lines splits a bent angle into two alternate angles.
- With algebra, use a rule to write an equation, solve it, then answer the actual question.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, AB = AC and ∠BAC = 40°. Find x, the size of ∠ACB.
questions.explanation: The base angles share 180 − 40 = 140°, so each is 70°. 140° is the total of both base angles, not one of them.
steps: AB = AC (tick marks), so the triangle is isosceles and ∠ABC = ∠ACB.
The two base angles together make 180 − 40 = 140° (angle sum of triangle).
Each base angle is 140 ÷ 2 = 70°, so x = 70°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 180 − 40 = 140 is the total of BOTH base angles — halve it.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the equal angles are the base angles at B and C, not the apex angle at A.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the angles of a triangle add to 180°, not 90° — start from 180 − 40.

questions.prompt: The two lines with arrows are parallel. Find x.
questions.explanation: The 115° angle is copied to the bottom crossing (corresponding angles), and x is vertically opposite that copy, so x = 115°. 65° would be the angle next to it on the straight line.
steps: At the bottom crossing, the angle above the line on the left of the transversal corresponds to the 115° angle, so it is 115° (corresponding, lines parallel).
x is vertically opposite that angle, so x = 115° (vertically opposite).

mistakes.A: Step 2: the corresponding angle is 115°, and x is vertically opposite it, so they are equal — they do not add to 180°.
mistakes.B: Step 2: vertically opposite angles are equal; do not subtract from 360°.
mistakes.D: Step 1: corresponding angles are equal — do not subtract 90°.

questions.diagram_alt: Two parallel lines cut by a transversal; at the top crossing the angle above the line on the left of the transversal is 115°, and at the bottom crossing the angle below the line on the right of the transversal is x

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 48° and ∠B = 67°. Side BC is extended to D. Find x, the exterior angle ∠ACD.
questions.explanation: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles: 48 + 67 = 115°. 65° is the interior angle at C, not the exterior one.
steps: The interior opposite angles to ∠ACD are ∠A and ∠B.
Exterior angle = sum of interior opposite angles, so x = 48 + 67 = 115°.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 65° is the angle inside the triangle at C. The exterior angle is the one outside, on the straight line with it.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the exterior angle equals the sum of BOTH interior opposite angles, 48° and 67°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the exterior angle is 48 + 67; do not subtract from 360°.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with angle A of 48° and angle B of 67°; side BC is extended to D and the exterior angle ACD is labelled x

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD. ∠BAE = 38° and ∠DCE = 47°. Find x, the size of ∠AEC.
questions.explanation: A construction line through E parallel to AB makes two Z shapes, so x = 38 + 47 = 85°. 95° comes from wrongly subtracting from 180°.
steps: Draw a line through E parallel to AB and CD — a construction line.

mistakes.A: Step 4: the bend angle is the SUM of the two parts, 38 + 47 — do not subtract it from 180°.
mistakes.B: Step 4: the two parts of the bend angle add together; do not find their difference.
mistakes.C: Step 4: x is the angle inside the bend, which is less than 180°. 275° is the reflex angle on the outside.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD with a bent line from A to E to C between them; angle BAE is 38°, angle DCE is 47°, and angle AEC is x

questions.prompt: In the diagram, AB = AC and side BC is extended to D. The exterior angle ∠ACD = 112°. Find x, the size of ∠BAC.
questions.explanation: ∠ACB = 180 − 112 = 68°, so ∠ABC = 68° too and x = 180 − 136 = 44°. 68° is the base angle, not the apex.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 68° is the base angle ∠ACB. You still need ∠BAC = 180 − 68 − 68.
mistakes.C: Step 1: halving 112° assumes ∠A = ∠B, but the equal angles are ∠B and ∠C (opposite the equal sides).
mistakes.D: Step 3: 68 + 68 = 136 is the sum of the base angles — subtract it from 180°.

questions.diagram_alt: Isosceles triangle ABC with tick marks showing AB equals AC; side BC is extended to D; the exterior angle ACD is 112° and angle A is labelled x

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, ∠A = x° and ∠B = (x + 20)°. Side BC is extended to D and ∠ACD = (3x − 10)°. Find x.
questions.explanation: The exterior angle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles: x + x + 20 = 3x − 10, so x = 30. Adding all three to 180° (giving 34) wrongly treats the exterior angle as part of the triangle.
steps: Exterior angle = sum of interior opposite angles: x + (x + 20) = 3x − 10.
Subtract 2x from both sides and add 10 to both sides: 30 = x. Check: 30 + 50 = 80 and 3 × 30 − 10 = 80 ✓

mistakes.A: Step 1: the exterior angle is outside the triangle, so do not add it to the angles inside. Use exterior = sum of interior opposite angles.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the equation is 2x + 20 = 3x − 10; you changed the −10 to +10.
mistakes.D: Step 3: −x = −30 means x is positive 30 — an angle size cannot be negative.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with angle A labelled x°, angle B labelled (x + 20)°, and side BC extended to D with exterior angle ACD labelled (3x − 10)°

questions.prompt: The two lines with arrows are parallel. P is on the top line; Q, R and S are on the bottom line. The angle between the top line (left of P) and PQ is 64°, and ∠PRS = 118°. Find x, the size of ∠QPR.
questions.explanation: ∠PQR = 64° (alternate angles), and the exterior angle 118° = 64 + x, so x = 54°. 62° is ∠PRQ, a different angle.
steps: The exterior angle ∠PRS = ∠PQR + ∠QPR (exterior angle of triangle PQR).

mistakes.A: Step 2: 62° is ∠PRQ. You still need the angle at P.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the 64° angle and ∠PQR form a Z (alternate angles), so they are equal — they do not add to 180°.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 64° is ∠PQR, the angle at Q. x is at P.

questions.diagram_alt: Two parallel lines; triangle PQR has P on the top line and Q and R on the bottom line, which continues to S; the angle between the top line on the left of P and PQ is 64°, angle QPR is x, and angle PRS is 118°

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD, and X and Y are on the parallel lines to the left of A and C. ∠XAE = 142° and ∠YCE = 125°. Find x, the size of ∠AEC.
questions.explanation: ∠BAE = 180 − 142 = 38° and ∠DCE = 180 − 125 = 55°, so the bend angle is 38 + 55 = 93°. Adding 142 + 125 = 267° skips the straight-line step.
steps: Draw a line through E parallel to AB and CD; it splits ∠AEC into two alternate angles, 38° and 55°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 142 + 125 is not the bend angle. First turn each given angle into the angle on the other side: 180 − 142 and 180 − 125.
mistakes.B: Step 3: you found 180 − 93. The bend angle is the sum of the two smaller angles, 38 + 55.
mistakes.C: Step 1: subtracting the two given angles uses no angle rule. Find ∠BAE and ∠DCE first (straight lines).

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines with points X, A, B on the top line and Y, C, D on the bottom line; a bent line runs from A to E to C; angle XAE is 142°, angle YCE is 125°, and angle AEC is x

questions.prompt: The two lines with arrows are parallel. The co-interior angles are (3x + 10)° and (2x − 5)°. Find the size of the larger angle.
questions.explanation: Co-interior angles add to 180°: 5x + 5 = 180, so x = 35 and the angles are 115° and 65°. 35 is the value of x, not an angle.

mistakes.A: Step 3: x = 35 is not an angle in the diagram — substitute it into 3x + 10.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 65° is the smaller angle, 2x − 5. The question asks for the larger one.

questions.diagram_alt: Two parallel lines cut by a transversal; between the lines on the right of the transversal, the angle at the top crossing is (3x + 10)° and the angle at the bottom crossing is (2x − 5)°

questions.prompt: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and ∠BAC = 36°. D is on AC so that BD = BC. Find x, the size of ∠ABD.
questions.explanation: Base angles are 72°, triangle BDC is isosceles so ∠BDC = 72° and ∠DBC = 36°, leaving x = 72 − 36 = 36°. 72° is all of ∠ABC, not part of it.
steps: In triangle BDC, BD = BC, so ∠BDC = ∠BCD = 72° (isosceles triangle).

mistakes.B: Step 1: 72° is the whole of ∠ABC. BD splits it into two parts — x is only the top part.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 108° is ∠ADB, the angle at D. x is at B.
mistakes.D: Step 3: BD does not cut ∠ABC in half. Use triangle BDC to find ∠DBC first.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle ABC with AB equal to AC (single ticks) and angle A of 36°; point D on AC is joined to B, with BD equal to BC (double ticks); angle ABD is labelled x

questions.prompt: AB ∥ CD. ∠BAE = 2x°, ∠DCE = 3x° and ∠AEC = 100°. Find the size of ∠BAE.
questions.explanation: The bend angle is the sum: 2x + 3x = 100, so x = 20 and ∠BAE = 40°. 20° is x itself, not 2x.
steps: A construction line through E parallel to AB splits ∠AEC into 2x° and 3x° (alternate angles).

mistakes.A: Step 3: x = 20 is not the angle asked for — ∠BAE is 2x.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 60° is ∠DCE = 3x. The question asks for ∠BAE = 2x.
mistakes.C: Step 1: the bend angle equals the SUM of the two angles (2x + 3x = 100); it is not 180 − 100.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel lines AB and CD with a bent line A to E to C; angle BAE is 2x°, angle DCE is 3x°, and angle AEC is 100°

questions.prompt: A light beam hits a flat mirror and bounces off. The beam going in and the beam coming out each make 28° with the mirror, as shown. Find x, the angle between the two beams.
questions.explanation: The three angles sit on the straight mirror line, so x = 180 − 28 − 28 = 124°. 56° is the sum of the two mirror angles, not the angle between the beams.
steps: The mirror is a straight line, and the 28°, x and 28° angles fill it with no gaps.
Angles on a straight line add to 180°: x = 180 − 28 − 28 = 124°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 28 + 28 = 56 is the two mirror angles. x is the rest of the straight line: subtract 56 from 180.
mistakes.C: Step 2: there are TWO 28° angles on the straight line; subtract both.
mistakes.D: Step 2: x is the whole angle between the beams — do not halve it.
